utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, Lorna Bolton, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Saxon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. And good morning to all the participants in the proceedings. On behalf of Mr. Perisic today are Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just -- yes. No, you go ahead, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I may have interrupted you. I was simply going to say that Ms. Bolton will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just before we do so, Ms. Bolton, one or two housekeeping matters. Today we are going to sit for two sessions only. I guess everybody is aware that that is almost a compulsion for all Judges to attend the plenary this afternoon. And on the 31st of March, again we are not sitting at all because of higher profile visitors to The Hague. Okay. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The next witness will be Ekrem Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just remind you before we get into the substance of your evidence, sir, that everything we say in court today is being translated and that it's necessary therefore to wait for simultaneous translation to be completed before you start answering the question. Okay?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I'd also remind you, sir, that because we are keeping a record of these proceedings, that it's always important to give a verbal response to the questions and not simply nod your head or shake your head. Okay?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on September 1st, 1959. I'm nearing the 50th.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that in terms of your educational background, that you completed high school and a post-secondary degree; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was your post-secondary degree in?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: After completing mechanical technical school in Sarajevo, I also graduated from mechanical engineering, so I'm a mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And following graduation, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Following graduation, I worked for ten years at a company called Zrak that is a special purpose company in Sarajevo. And following this, in 1993, I was transferred to the Republic Secretariat for the Interior of [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear the translation of the last word, the interior and I don't think the translator got it either. You were transferred to the Republic Secretariat for the Interior of?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, this is -- when you are talking about the Republic Secretariat, what department are we talking about? What kind of work? Bless you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] We are talking about the Republic Secretariat of the Interior following which it was -- it turned into a Federal Ministry of the Interior, so up until the war it was a the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then after the war, up until the moment it was transferred into -- or became the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, it functioned in that capacity. And I don't know exactly what year this transfer occurred in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And the Ministry of Interior, sir, am I correct that that was the ministry that had responsibility for policing services?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you indicated you were transferred there in 1993. To what department were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to the department for anti-terrorist protection. Or anti-sabotage protection, that's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Does it have an acronym of KDZ?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the acronym is KDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was your position when you first joined that unit back in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I came to the department for mines and explosives, following which I was the chief of the department for explosives.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When did you become the chief?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact date, but it was after the war, as far as I can recall. Just after the war ended, but I'm not absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. In your work then with the KDZ during the war, did you have occasion to be involved in conducting on-site investigations involving projectiles?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I took part in the investigations. I did not conduct them because they are conducted by an investigating judge, but I participated in the team that conducted the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And in terms of the on-site investigations, did you investigate any incidents involving mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Artillery shells?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, artillery shells as well, and basically we conducted all types of investigations, on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how about modified air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I also participated in on-site investigations with incidents involving modified air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just with respect to modified air-bombs, I don't wish to go into any specific details of any of the incidents, but could you tell us the approximate number of modified air-bomb incidents you were involved in investigating?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, officially I participated in two on-site investigations involving modified air-bombs. On one occasion I also went to the site where a modified air-bomb had struck but it did not explode. And then we also -- I also attended a site where a modified air-bomb fell into the river, so we could not complete that part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So that would appear to be approximately four in total then?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we cannot really talk about an on-site investigation in this event where I went after the event with a colleague because we just went to check out a report that a modified air-bomb had fallen into the river. And I'm not sure if there was a report prepared on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So that would be sort of an unofficial visit, not an official on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in addition to participating in on-site investigations, were you also involved in performing laboratory analyses of trace evidence recovered from some of these scenes of explosions?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did an analysis of trace evidence, but they weren't lab analyses in the true sense of the word. We didn't investigate the types of materiels, but we analysed the trace evidence to determine the type of projectiles that had left these trace evidence. So this was not -- this was done within our department. It wasn't a laboratory in the true sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come back to that in a little bit more detail later, sir, I just want to talk about your role in on-site investigations first. All right. What were the duties of the KDZ officers when they participated in an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: As a general rule, the main task was to recover trace evidence on the site itself. And this event where we are talking about projectiles, we would have to collect all evidence remaining after this projectile had hit the site where we came to do the on-site investigation. At the same time, we had to determine the direction from which the projectile had come.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how would you go about determining the direction from which the projectile had originated?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Each projectile when it strikes leaves a trace on the barrier or the surface that it hits, and the trace that is left behind is symmetrical. And by determining the axis to determine the symmetry of the trace, we determine the direction of the projectile flight. And based on the evidence around the crater, we determine the direction from which the projectile originated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So we are talking here about crater analysis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you would look for -- you told us first that when projectiles fall they leave an impression that is roughly symmetrical or symmetrical, and then you talked about locating an axis. What is the axis that you are locating?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the symmetric axis of the trace left by the projectile. In other words, the axis dividing the impression that was left by the projectile. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And if you are able to locate this, I'm going to call it the axis of symmetry, what does that then tell you about the direction from which the projectile originated?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This axis that we establish actually corresponds to the path of the flight of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is there any other evidence that you consider in determining the origin or the direction from which the projectile was fired?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In order to determine the direction, as far as I know, this is the only matter and way to determine the direction. In other words, this axis of symmetry. And as for determining the type of projectile, then you have to analyse the traces that you find on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about first of all when you arrive at a scene, is there any difference in the appearance of an impression or a crater that would be left by a mortar shell as compared to an artillery shell or a modified air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: There are differences. In the case of air-bombs, which are meant for destroying buildings, they produce huge craters on the impact site and they destroy the buildings on which they had fallen. There is also a difference between mortar and artillery shells. The impression itself looks different.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you -- are you able to articulate how they look different, mortar versus artillery?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The impressions of mortar shells are characteristic, we used to call them rosettas. And in the case of mortar shells, the specific thing is that they are fired from weapons, and they fly without rotating, as opposed to artillery shells which rotate during the flight, they rotate around their own axis.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And why would you call the impressions left by mortar shells rosettas?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know, I couldn't really answer that question. I know it's a very inappropriate name for such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What is a rosetta?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear about your question. Do you mean the impression, or?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, in common -- common parlance what is a rosetta?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: A rosetta or rose in B/C/S is something that actually looks like a rose, like a flower.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. In terms of -- you indicated to us, then, that the size of the crater obviously is something that is of interest to you, and you talked a little about the shape of the crater, and the differences. Can you tell me then what would be of interest to you in terms of the trace evidence?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of the trace evidence we collected, as far as that was possible in those wartime conditions, we collected and recovered all trace evidence that could be linked to the projectile that had landed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was then done with this evidence once collected?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The evidence was then submitted or sent to our department for analysis. I think there were cases where we would just take over these -- or collect these traces on the spot and prepare a report right there, but usually officers from the security centre would collect the evidence and then they would submit an official request to determine the type of projectile and forward it to us, to the Ministry of Interior to our department, where we would carry out an official analysis, or rather, determine the projectile that these traces come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So let's just talk about once you physically have the materiel in your department, do you use any equipment to examine the materiel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our department we had, and it was already there when I arrived in the department, we had samples of fuses from various projectiles, not all of course, and we also had and collected whenever we had occasion, samples of the projectiles themselves that had landed on the city but not exploded. And of course we would remove the explosive charge from the projectile and keep the bodies of the projectiles in order to be able to conduct a parallel analysis, a comparative analysis, and determine as accurately as we could the trace evidence that we found and the projectile they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the purpose then of -- if I understand your evidence, the purpose, then, of taking the pieces that you recovered and comparing them to unexploded projectiles is to determine the type of projectile; is that a fair summary of what you've told us?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just going back to the crater analysis portion, are you familiar with the term "angle of impact"?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what does the term "angle of impact" refer to?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: During the on-site investigations I did not really work on determining the angle of impact, but each projectile is fired under certain degree and it also lands at a certain degree. It lands and hits the surface at a certain degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So you weren't involved, I take it, in the actual calculation of the angle of impact in those investigations where it was possible to make that calculation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I was not involved on determining the angle of impact, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't know if you can answer this question, but do you know if it was always possible to determine an angle of impact or not?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my opinion is that if all the parameters that are used in calculating the angle of impact, then I think in most cases it is possible to determine this. So you need to have -- to establish certain parameters and then they would be mathematically calculated to determine the angle of impact. The angle at which the projectile hit the surface.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you are talking about parameters, what are you talking about? What would be the parameters you would need to know?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are calculations, as far as I know. You have to calculate the dimensions of the crater, or rather, the traces left by shrapnel, but you also have to determine the centre of the explosive charge and the projectile. And I think these are the parameters you need in order to calculate the angle of impact. It's possible there are some other parameters, but I really was not involved in this and I could not give you any more details.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on to discuss a specific incident with you, sir, and that was an incident relating to explosions at the flea market on the 22nd of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in that regard could we please have Prosecution Exhibit 415 displayed, please. In the B/C/S version, could we -- we have the cover page displayed, could we now move forward to page 5 in e-court. And I believe that corresponds with page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the document that's displayed before you?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter -- as a general rule. This is one of the official reports compiled by one of the colleagues from the CSB after an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And this is an official report in relation to an explosion on the 22nd December, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, didn't mean to interrupt you, sir. And when we met last week, you had the opportunity to review the entire report; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do the contents of that report accord with your recollection of the investigation that was conducted.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This report also mentions the individuals who were on site in the on-site -- on the on-site team and then there is also a brief report on the on-site investigation completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And do the contents of the report in terms of the findings that were made, having had the opportunity to review the report, do you still agree with the conclusions that were reached?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Both the report and the analysis of the fragments following this, the analysis that followed, completely accord with what is stated here and as written down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could move forward in e-court in the B/C/S version only to page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a report that we compiled in the department itself on the investigation of the trace evidence following an explosion on the 22nd of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, you would agree that this is not the best copy of the report, it's difficult to read? Sorry, sir, we need a verbal response.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's not the best of copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I would like to bring up 65 ter 1439.01, please. And if you could bring up the English translation of that as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the document that you see in front of you now, sir, 1439.01, how does it compare with the document we were just looking at which is part of Exhibit P415?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a report about an on-site investigation. It's just that this is a better copy, but it is actually one and the same report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could move forward to page 2 of this report in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We see on the B/C/S version, sir, the initials ES. Can you tell me whose initials those are?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: These are my initials.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Does that mean that you prepared this report, sir?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about this investigation, sir, and if at any point you need to refresh your memory, would you please let -- from the documents, would you please let us know.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall how many projectiles exploded at the flea market on the 22nd of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Two projectiles exploded in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what is the name of the flea market that we are talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could perhaps go back one page in each report, that may assist the witness in refreshing his memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Does that assist you at all, sir, or do we need to go back to the main report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This doesn't help because this flea market was operational during the war. It didn't exist before the war. There was no market in the area, as far as I can remember. And here we can simply see what were the names of the streets at the time where these projectiles impacted. Telali is one of the street, the former street of Petra Kocica. Whether the flea market was named after the street, I can't really remember. I really don't remember whether there was an official name of the flea market.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can we bring Prosecution 415 back up on the screen, please. And if we could display page 18 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, before we do that what do you intend doing with this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I have some further questions about this report. I'll come back to it. I will eventually be seeking to have it tendered. I've only asked for the B/C/S version with respect to this page, Your Honours, because there is no equivalent page in the English version, it being a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the area that is circled on page 18 of the B/C/S version of your report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a map of a part of Sarajevo and in this circle we can see the site of this flea market where these two projectiles fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you tell us how densely or sparsely populated that area was during the war?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the old part of town. Before the war and after the war, it was always very densely populated. This is close to Bascarsija, the very centre of the old Sarajevo. So this is just off the very centre of Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. When you arrived on scene on the 22nd December, 1994, do you recall what the scene looked like?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to remember all the details after so many years. This was not the only on-site investigation I participated in, but anyway, whenever we came to the site where projectiles impacted, usually there were very few people around because during the shelling usually shells kept on falling after the first ones, so people tried to hide away from possible continued shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you review the photographic portion of this brief before your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I reviewed the photographs taken during the on-site investigation following the impact of these two projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did the photographs capture the scene as you recall it, or are you able to comment 15 years later?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: On the photographs, you can see parts of the projectiles that were collected on the two places of impact, so these parts were collected and a photograph was taken. The remaining of the photographic documentation also includes pictures of dead persons, of persons killed. Also from their autopsies and so on, but this was not my purview. What we reviewed were the craters, the impact signs and the parts of the shells that were photographed on the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall with respect to this incident whether you found any evidence to suggest that this marketplace had been -- was in use by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't find evidence of that kind, but as far as I know, nowhere in the vicinity was there a military facility or military installation. The closest facility was the command post, the HQ of the former Yugoslav People's Army but this was, again, on the other side of the river, so it was rather far away. As far as my knowledge goes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned there were some people killed, to the best of your recollection were any of those people wearing ABiH uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember without seeing the pictures. I can't really say whether they were or not. But in the markets regularly you would also find people wearing uniforms, people who came back from the front-lines, they would also go to the market. So you could find people in uniforms also in the markets, but these were not military units, these were individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could have displayed, please, pages 17 of the report. Again just in the B/C/S version as it is a drawing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this drawing, sir?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the drawing of the site on which you can see two places marked where these projectiles impacted. In the bottom right angle of the corner, this was the market itself. Across the street you can see a tram stop, and next to the tram stop there were some small private shops. A line of small private shops.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you indicate, please, what numbers on this -- what the numbers 1 and 2 on this drawing -- what they are showing or marking?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Numbers 1 and 2 are places of impact of the projectiles. One is marked with number 1 and the other one is marked with number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you perform or participate in performing the crater analysis in this case?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I participated in the crater analysis. The -- nobody did the crater analysis on his own. It was always done in segments. And as far as I know, it was me and a colleague of mine from my department, we determined the trajectory of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could bring up 1439.01 again, please. If we could go to page 2 of both versions, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, there's an indication in this report that the determination was made as to the direction or origin of fire. Could you tell us what the report indicates?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In this report it is stated that the projectile was fired from the direction determined by the azimuth angle 159.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you are talking about an azimuth angle, and with the number 159, what is the -- it's 159 of what unit? What is the unit of measure?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I didn't get any translation of that, am I the only one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the angle measured clock-wise from the line of true north to the line of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how does that line and that azimuth, how would that compare with the axis of symmetry that you talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, this is an angle between the north and the axis of symmetry measured from the axis of north in a clock-wise direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And where, then, having plotted the axis of symmetry using the azimuth, where did you determine the likely origin or direction of fire was from?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: When you determine the axis of symmetry on the spot, it is visible, but then you use this azimuth to transfer this to the map in order to be able to show on the map the precise trajectory of the projectile, and that map was an element of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. When you plotted it on the map in this case, from what area did the -- what area on the map, then, did you indicate the direction of fire was from?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The projectile was fired from the area of Trebevic, and the azimuth angle can determine it much more precisely because Trebevic is a large mountain but on the basis of the azimuth, you can determine very clearly where from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And which army's positions in the area of Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Trebevic, there were the separation lines. However, the largest portion of the mountain was controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your report indicates that the projectile was fired or corresponds to the direction of the enemies' position in the area of Trebevic, I'm wondering if you then would have considered the location of the two armies in coming to that conclusion at the time?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not understand very clearly your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps if we go to the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: First of all, could I have this exhibit tendered, please, as a -- or this document tendered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document, 1439.01, is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could return to Exhibit P415, and if we could bring up page 13 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you okay, sir? Would you like some water or can we help you with anything? You have been coughing quite a bit, I'm concerned about your health.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I'm fine. I had a slight cold recently and I took some medicines to cure that but now I'm fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the map that's displayed before you, there is an area which I think is marked, looks like with a number 3. Do you see the area between two lines?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What would that area be?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The marked area is the area between the place where the projectile fell and Trebevic, so this is an area wherefrom the projectile was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And why isn't it just -- why are there two lines? We talked about plotting the azimuth on the map. Why is there more than one line?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: When you determine the trajectory axis, it is impossible to be entirely precise. This is why you always have a tolerance in order to eliminate any mistakes, so we used to do it with plus/minus 5 degrees in comparison to the azimuth as measured on the site. So this is the tolerance for possible error in measurement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Now that you see the plotting on the map, sir, does that assist you in recalling which army's positions -- from which army's positions the projectile originated?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't determine precisely the spot where the projectile was fired from because we were not aware of the conditions under which the projectiles were fired, but I believe that this came from the region that was controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we please go back to Exhibit P2217. And could we go to page 2 of the B/C/S version. And you can leave the -- sorry, we were on page 2 of the English version, that was fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I want to ask you, sir, what conclusion was reached as to the type and calibre of shell that caused the two explosions?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In this case, these were two artillery shells, 76 millimetres with UTI M68 fuses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you told us -- well, we've talked about the fact that mortar shells and artillery shells aren't the same. In terms of their appearance, how do they differ in appearance, a mortar shell versus an artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: They are not the same. Mortar shell, as I said, fly without any rotation. They are simply fired from the barrel and they also have a stabiliser. We used to call it a tail-fin. So this tail-fin stabilises the flight of the projectile through the air. Whereas artillery shells that are fired from Howitzers or artillery guns, their flight direction is kept by the rotation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do artillery shells have fins or stabilisers?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Artillery shells do not have fins. They have rings, guidance rings used during the firing to get the proper rotation of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you investigated explosions caused by mortar shells, how often would you find pieces of the fins or stabilisers?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In most cases the tail part should always be found. However, given the conditions in which we carried out on-site investigation, sometimes if the projectile went into the ground, sometimes we simply did not have enough time and it was too dangerous to carry out a proper investigation as it would have been done in peacetime. So we didn't dig for it if we found sufficient amount of other evidence which would indicate to the type of the projectile. But in most cases, the stabilisers, the tail-fins were found when we had mortars impacting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if you found those pieces, is that something that would be recorded in your reports?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say for certain whether my colleagues who conducted the on-site investigation entered in the reports because that was not part of my job. But we would receive reports with the trace evidence and then usually there would be mention of that portion in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I should have been more specific, sir. If you in examining the fragments, the traces, after the fact found pieces of a fin, is that something that you would personally put in your reports?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: We did not prepare individual reports, on-site investigation reports, because it was unnecessary for everyone to do their own report. There was one general report, on-site investigation report. I don't know about the investigating judge, but as far as our work on site there was one report. We prepared a report following an analysis of the trace evidence per an official request from the CSB, and in that report of ours, usually we would also mention what types of trace evidence we received to investigate or analyse.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In this report there's an indication that you found or that you were able to identify a UTI M68 fuse. Are UTI M68 fuses used, to the best of your knowledge, in 82-calibre mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I never found in any bibliography that these fuses are used, so when we analysed the trace evidence, in addition to using the traces found there, we also used to compare this or to read up on this from various materiels. And as far as I can recall, I never came across any article where these fuses were mentioned as being used.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR also attend the scene of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, did the UNPROFOR officers seize any of the trace evidence?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, they never seized any trace evidence. They only photographed the site itself, and I know that they also conducted their own measurements and tried to determine the direction where the projectile originated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In terms of your reaching of the conclusions as stated in this report as to the fact that this was an M-70 76 millimetre calibre artillery shell, how important was your analysis of the trace evidence in arriving at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, where do we get it that it's artillery?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's something he has already stated earlier in his verbal evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, was my last question translated to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was translated. On principle or generally speaking, all of this is artillery, but in this particular case, these were not mortar shells but artillery gun shells or Howitzer shells. But in this particular case, this was an air-gun shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. My question, sir, was: In coming to that conclusion as to what type of projectile that was, how important or unimportant was the actual analysis of the trace evidence in coming to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the analysis of the trace evidence was significant and important when you were to draw conclusions as to what shells these fragments were from, but if we found the stabiliser, and as I've already mentioned we did in most cases, this made the job easier. We analysed other trace evidence as well, but the stabiliser itself was significant because it would actually indicate what calibre shell this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to confuse things. Was a stabiliser found in this case?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In this case there were two shells, but no stabiliser was found in either case. And I just need to add that had it been a mortar shell or had these been mortar shells, in my view, a stabiliser would have had to be found because the ground where the shell struck was asphalt or concrete. So the stabiliser would not be embedded in the soil or ground, and we didn't need to dig in order to find it. So in my view in this particular instance, we would have had to find the stabilisers but we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I was going to move on to another area very quickly, sir, which just has to do with what you told us earlier about the modified air-bomb incidents you were aware of. And one of the things you indicated is that in an unofficial capacity you went to a modified air-bomb incident where a bomb fell in a river?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the river-bed of the Miljacka river above the old part of town. Stream.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were there any military installations in the river?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, as far as I know there were no installations of any sort. It is possible that -- it's probable that the lines of separation were somewhere in that area, but I know that when I went there, I did not observe any installation, either military or civilian. This was in the vicinity, it's very close to the old town. I think this locality is called Dariva. I think it was in that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, sir. In this case --

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Dariva.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In this case, do you believe that the modified air-bomb hit its intended target?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really believe that this type of question cannot be put to the witness. This is calling for guess-work on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Other than -- you've indicated there didn't appear to be any military installations in the river, was there any other apparent military purpose that would have been served by landing a modified air-bomb in the river in that location, based on your observations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a reworded question but its essence is the same. On page 25, line 14, the witness said that he was not aware that there were any military or civilian installations there, and I think this is really calling -- or leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's a leading question because there's no facts or suggested answer being put to the witness. What was objectionable, I think, about the last question was that perhaps I was asking him to speculate as to what was -- what the intentions were of the persons sending the projectile, and here, I think, in the question as currently worded, I've corrected that deficiency in the original question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stand by my objection. I think this is calling for this witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you recall my question now, sir, or do I need to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I can recall your question. I think I said earlier that this type of projectile were meant for destruction of installations, and I think there was no point in firing it on this particular location. That's my opinion. Even if some lines were there, that type of projectile would have had no effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question to you, sir, had been, was there any military purpose that could have been served by firing the projectile to where it was fired. I would imagine that your answer would be yes, there was some kind of military purpose, or no, or I don't know. One of those three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was no military purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just a couple more questions in this area. I'm conscious of the time, Your Honour. Just wonder, if Mr. Usher, you could assist the witness in being able to draw a sketch in our computer programme. I'm going to be asking him to draw a sketch of what a -- the pieces of a modified air-bomb look like. So I guess I need a blank piece of paper in essence and a pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to be able to do that in a minute?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: After the break, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I would hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've got only one minute to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Only one minute, yes. We'll draw quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Try to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot draw parts of a projectile. I can draw a representation of this bomb, of what it looks like. Usually this air-bomb also has stabilisers, but in this case, as far as we could determine during these on-site investigations, the bombs would be modified because certain adapted elements would be affixed to it, in other words, rocket engines. And in all the cases where I was, there were four rocket engines that were attached to the bomb, and they actually carried the projectile to the point of impact. If that is what you were looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It is. And I just want to quickly label what you've drawn here. On the far right of the diagram you've got a series of, looks like, four cylinders. What do those represent?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I tried to draw here were three cylinders. These represent rocket engines for multiple rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And in the middle of the diagram there is a small -- a small area that seems to connect the rockets to something else. What is that area?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: We would find a plate on the site, the plate connecting the air-bomb to the rocket engines, so the only purpose was to attach these and make them one compact whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the front part of your diagram then, I take it, is the actual bomb part; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the left-hand side, that's the bomb itself. The body of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And very quickly can you put a 1 on the bomb.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: A 2 next to the connecting plate.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And a 3 next to the rockets, please.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if that could be marked as the next exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That sketch is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And we don't have a corresponding 65 ter number for this. You will be able to know, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It would be a convenient time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just before we leave the area of modified air-bombs, sir, before the break we were talking about the existence of a metal plate that connects the rocket portion and the bomb portion in a modified air-bomb. Were there any other projectiles in use during the conflict that had that metal plate?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move on to the final area of your evidence which has to do with the examination of traces to determine the place and date of manufacture.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I have P656, please. Madam Registrar, I'm going to need the second page of each of these -- each version of this report, please. And for the record, this is investigation into an incident on the 22nd of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And again, we see the initials ES on the B/C/S version of this report, sir. Whose initials would those be?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see them. They are mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the KDZ department who would have been signing reports with the initials ES?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to -- sorry, again, sir, given that your initials are on the report, does that mean that you performed the analysis of the trace evidence in relation to this projectile?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I conducted this analysis, although we had frequently consultations, I with my colleagues, but in this particular instance it was my job to complete this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Right. I'm interested, sir, in the portion of your report where you discuss some markings that were found on the stabiliser of a mortar projectile. Your report indicates there was impressed marking KB 9502. First, can you tell us would the letters have been in Latin script or Cyrillic script or some other script?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: These markings, in this particular instance, were in Cyrillic. In other words, what it says here is KV 9502. That is why it is in parenthesis because we've just copied what we found on the part that was under analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, a B in Cyrillic script correlates to what letter in Latin script?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The B in the Latin script corresponds to a V sound or letter in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And what do the initials KB tell you about the place of manufacture of this shell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to add something before I answer your question. The projectiles were marked by manufacturer, and all those special-purpose factories or, rather, military contractors had their own markings. In this particular case, this means the Krusik factory in Valjevo, in the town of Valjevo which is in Serbia. The numeric portion of this marking in the case of these projectiles, the first two digits indicate the year of manufacture, and the latter two digits indicate the series, the serial number or the batch of the projectile when it was manufactured.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could bring up, please, Exhibit P676.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, did you get an answer to your question at line 10, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, my question at line 10, Your Honour? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, he said, "I would just like to add something before I answer your question." At line 14 that's what he says. And you had just asked a question prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: But just for clarification, the K, the initial K would correspond to what, and the initial B would correspond to what?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: K corresponds to the factory name. That's Krusik. And V or B is Valjevo. That is the place where the factory was. So in this particular case, this was a projectile from that factory. In other cases they would have had different markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were calling for something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, it was P676, please. With the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. This is Exhibit P676, is it? Thank you. If I could have the second page again of each.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And again on the B/C/S version, sir, you just confirm whether those are your initials, ES?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in this report there was an indication that with respect to a 120-millimetre mortar shell there were found embossed in Cyrillic script the letters "MK, M74 KB9503." You've told us what the KB and the 95 and the 03 would relate to. Do the initials MK or M74 add anything or correspond to anything that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the shell itself, and M74 is a model, as it were. The model from 1974.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I don't intend to take you, sir, through all the reports you authored in this regard. I do wish to take you to some where there are differences or unique characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So could I have Exhibit P677, please. Could we have the second page of both the English and the B/C/S versions, please. And I may have -- actually if you go back to the first page, please, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In the English translation, sir, and I think this is displayed at the bottom of the page in B/C/S, there is an indication that the trace evidence in this case was scrutinized by use of a magnifying-glass and all necessary measurements were performed. What would you have been measuring?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: If a fragment is delivered that still has some portion of the fuse or stabiliser, we would compare the thread --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The tread, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although it was something that could be determined by just looking at it. You could determine by just looking at the portion of the shell what type of shell it belonged to, but we also tried to determine the diametre of the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And that kind of information, that kind of detail, what would that assist you in determining?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Usually the parts where the fuses are attached to can differ on various shells, so because we had unspent shells, we tried to compare whether the particular portion corresponded to some unspent shell in order to determine as precisely as we could what the projectile was. In this particular case where we only had the metal portion with the tail-fins, we measured the diameter of the stabiliser and the depth, or rather, or how thick the tin was and then based on that we could determine what shell it came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. In the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I think we'll need to flip to page 2 in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's an indication of a marking "MK, M74 KB9309." What does the 93 tell us?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The 93 indicates the year of manufacture of the shell. In other words, this was manufactured in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And the next paragraph refers to a book, Ammunition or Imunicija. What was the use that was made of that book by your department?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that in addition to the samples of shells and fuses that we used, we also used books, and in this particular book, it gives a description of all types of projectiles. In part one mortar shells are described, whereas part two describes artillery shells other than mortar shells. In other words, there is a detailed description of the shells and what type of fuses can be used for which type of shell. In other words, this is a military book. It was published by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence of the former Yugoslavia. That's what the acronym SSNO stands for.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. If we could move on to Exhibit P659, please. And if you could scroll down on the page for us, please, to the B/C/S version. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you indicate, sir, whether this was an incident in relation to which you participated in the on-site investigation as well as the analysis of the shell fragments?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I was present on the scene; you can see that from this report. I'm not sure in which particular activities I participated. I can't remember that now, but I certainly was present on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could move forward in both versions to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is an indication in the English version that in this case a determination was made as to the origin or the likely direction from which the shell or shells were fired. And can you tell me, would the method that was used to make that determination differ -- in this case have differed in any way from the method that you've described earlier in your evidence with respect to crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The method is always the same, and this is the only method that can be used. You have to find the axis of symmetry in the impact left by the projectile. And this report was not compiled by me, it was compiled by somebody who was tasked to do that from the investigating team. And here very briefly you can see the composition of the team present on the site and in the continuation of the text you can see the list of people who were killed, injured, and so on. So it was not compiled by me personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: One thing I do note is that we have an indication that this was a 120-millimetre artillery projectile, and I am looking at the paragraph that starts with the words "On 21.06.1995." And then later in that same paragraph we have the description of the crater as being a rose. And I thought I understood you say earlier that mortar shells left roses. Can you -- did I misunderstand you earlier?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, here we also have a mortar shell, but, as I said, it all belongs to the artillery. Both artillery guns and mortar guns, it all together belongs to artillery. So here we had a mortar shell, a 120 millimetre that was fired from a mortar gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So a mortar is a -- although the shells vary, it can still be described as a type of artillery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that in military terminology and literature, it belongs under the title of artillery. I'm not an artillery expert but I believe it belongs to artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when we see in reports the use of the phrase "the aggressor's positions," what army are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Here it refers to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With indulgence. If we could bring up Exhibit 669, please. If we could turn to the last page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The question probably seems obvious, sir, but when we see in the final or near to the end of this report an indication that the direction of fire corresponds to the direction of enemy positions in the greater area of Miljevici, when we are talking about enemy positions, what army would we be referring to?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: We are referring to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And finally, if we could bring up Exhibit P660. If we could turn to, please, page 4 of the English version. Page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On the B/C/S version, sir, there's a signature at the bottom left of the page. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And with respect to this report, if we could move forward, please, two pages in the B/C/S version only. Can you zoom in sort of on the bottom half of the map, please, Madam Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is a marking on this map, sir, that says "AZ" or "2 equals 298." Could you tell me what that is short for or what that indicates?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the trajectory and the azimuth angle that was measured on the spot, and the azimuth was 298 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in this case given that you had signed the report, does that mean that you would have prepared the map?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And going back to the page 3 of the B/C/S version of the report and page 4 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There are conclusions reached in this report with respect to the indication that the direction corresponds to the direction of the enemy positions in the general area of Doglode. Would that have been a conclusion that you reached, sir, or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, I came to this conclusion having drawn the trajectory on the map, the trajectory as determined by the azimuth angle measured on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In this type of report that I've been showing you, for example, the report we are talking about now, if you had -- if there had been any evidence that the shell had landed on a military installation, is that something that we would expect to find in this report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I never participated in an on-scene investigation when a shell landed on a military installation. So in the report you would mark all the important activities, but I never participated in an on-scene investigation concerning projectiles that fell on military installation. I don't know whether this was done by the army, but those of us from the police, we only carried out investigations when projectiles hit the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in any given week -- work week for you during the hostilities, how many shell investigations or shelling investigations might you be involved in typically?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really determine the number. I can't really be very precise here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Average, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately over 50 or 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In a week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Total. During the time I worked in this particular department and during the hostilities. So this was the number of on-site investigations. It shouldn't necessarily correspond to the number of reports I compiled because if I was participating in an on-site investigation, I wasn't necessarily writing a corresponding report myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bolton. Madam Bolton, just before you sit down, did the status of this witness change from a 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear the end part of your question, sir. Did the status of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Change from a 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Oh, it did, yes. He did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It did. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Suljevic. My name is Novak Lukic, and on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Perisic, I will now ask several questions.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please make sure to allow some time after my question in order for the interpreters to be able to interpret my question and I will do the same before asking the following question.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you started working in the police, you said you worked in a factory in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the location of this factory in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The factory Zrak is located in Buca Potok, this is one part of the town of Sarajevo in the municipality Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far is it from the municipal building of the municipality of Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: These are on -- located on two different edges of the municipality of Novi Grad. Without having a proper map, I couldn't tell the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was a special purpose factory which means that it produced for the needs of the former JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the former JNA and for the export, but it was military production.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the facility itself, the premises of the factory were controlled by the Army of the BiH before the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the war the factory worked with reduced capacity, but it continued to produce; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The production was much reduced. Now, what could be produced under given conditions without proper resources or raw materials, that's another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you did until the year 1993 when you worked for the factory had nothing to do with your later job in the Ministry of the Interior, so while you were in the factory, you were not involved with artillery, ammunition or other things that you talked about here today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And while you worked for the factory you were not involved in any training or professional development concerning the ballistic investigation that you later participated in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you heard -- do you know that during the war from the premises of the factory Zrak, the BiH Army fired shells against the positions of Republika Srpska Army, so do you know that they used these premises?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the factory called Zica?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where it was located in comparison to the assembly building of the municipality of Novi Grad? Was it closer than the factory Zrak?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was closer, but it was on the same side of the river as factory Zrak, but it was considerably closer to the assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was also located in the territory controlled by the BiH Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have over half an hour, but if you do not feel well, you can ask for a recess. If not, we can continue for half an hour, I'll try to finish this today.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your concern. I think I can manage that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, you did not participate in any training concerning ballistic theory or what you engaged in when you started to work for the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Officially no training was organised, but before I started to participate in investigations on my own, I participated in investigations carried out by my colleagues who worked in the same department before I started to work there. So in a way I learned through work, through practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you learned by doing?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I also learned a theory from my colleagues in the department, but there was no officially organised training.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you -- have you been tested? Did you take any examination?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such examination. I don't know that it exists. I don't know that there is any official training in this particular field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand from your testimony, the core issue, the most important issue to determine the trajectory of a projectile is a crater analysis, so analysis of the crater left by the projectile?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When analysing a crater, is it necessary to determine the centre of the crater in order to be able to determine the axis of symmetry, the azimuth, and all that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the trajectory has to go through the very centre of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the investigation, was it necessary to mark the centre of the crater by some form of marking?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The very centre of the crater we did not mark, but visually you could determine it on the spot and you could determine it precisely enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you take a photograph of the crater on the spot, I assume that this is done by crime scene investigators?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to be able to verify the trajectory of the projectile later on, is it necessary to take a photograph of the crater with some kind of marking in the vicinity so that later on you can compare this photograph to the real situation?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't really answer that question. I believe that the wider scene was also photographed, but as you photograph the crater itself, if there is a point for orientation that it will be encompassed by the photograph. If there is nothing else there, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is that in order for somebody to be able later on to determine the trajectory in comparison to the points of the compass, wouldn't it be necessary to have something else on the photograph beside the crater itself because on the basis of the crater itself, you cannot compare this to anything and you cannot verify your finding from the scene?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: On the scene it was sufficient to measure the azimuth of the determined trajectory, and then you know how any map is oriented. It's oriented on the basis of the north, so later on you can provide the map along with your report and you draw the trajectory on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we kindly look at a photograph so maybe my question will become clearer. So Exhibit P415, page 28, please, if we could have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is part of crime file regarding the incident that you were involved in. When we look at this photograph, there are no markings of any kind made by the on-site investigators as to the direction from which the projectile had arrived; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the next photograph on the next page, please. Page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this photograph we do see an indication, there's a number 1 there marked, there is a marker of sorts.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is an arrow as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. That's an arrow. What is this arrow supposed to indicate?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please just scroll this photograph up a bit because there is a caption under the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it says there: "The photograph of the centre of explosion, photographed from the direction of the impact of the projectile marked with an arrow." Correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, to go back to my earlier question, based on this photograph, if I were to compare your findings in view of the fact that there is no other landmark or point of reference on the basis of which I can determine this direction, there is no way that I can compare this to your findings. I cannot compare this photograph or superimpose it on the map to determine the direction; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not based on this photograph. But the direction that was determined on the spot was later analysed and we determined the area from which the projectile was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you agree with me that this marking indicating the direction -- marking the direction as determined from where the projectile had come, would have been easier if there was another reference point in the photograph, for instance, the wall of a building or something of that sort that is of a permanent nature?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a wall of a building would not really be much of a reference point because right now there are all sorts of different buildings there, so it wouldn't be possible to determine it.
