But you cannot see any of the shops that were lined up there, but you can see the traces left, the impressions left by the fragments, they were marked in chalk, and you can see that based on that, we were able to determine the axis of symmetry which is an indication of the path of the projectile flight. And as for this photograph itself, it is true that you cannot determine anything else based on the photograph only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the gist of my question. I was asking you whether based on this photograph you could determine the direction of the projectile, where the projectile came from, in order to check what was indicated there with this arrow. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not based on this photograph because this is just a photograph of a crater with the compass and the arrow pointing to the direction. In other words, part and parcel of this photograph is also a map and the sketch of the site itself, based on the photograph alone, you cannot determine that but that is why this whole job was done by a larger group of people because there were members of the on-site investigation team who collected the trace evidence, others drew sketches of the scene and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Suljevic, completely. You've already explained this, but my question was this: If I suspected that you did not correctly determine the azimuth, for instance, I could not check that and determine the actual azimuth based on this photograph alone; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. You couldn't because the photographs were not made with that purpose in mind. But I would like to add here that irrespective of us and independently of us there were also members of the UNPROFOR who came to the scene and they also calculated the direction on their own. And then when we compared the findings, they actually corresponded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll get back to that, but I just had some general questions and I wanted to use these documents to explore those areas. Tell us, please, in your work, you had to perform two types of analysis, generally speaking. One of those was to analyse the materiel traces found on the scene and based on those traces, you were supposed to give your opinion on the type of projectile, what calibre, and the likely manufacturer of that particular shell. That was one aspect of your work; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The other aspect of your work was if you were requested to come to the scene, you were supposed to try to determine the direction from which the shell was fired; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there instances where you were requested to determine the direction from which the projectile was fired without going on the site itself? In other words, to determine it based on some other documents that were forwarded to you, for instance, photographs?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. We never received any photographs attached to these requests to perform an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You only received fragments; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, fragments alone. And in some instances we did not even determine the direction, because that was not part of the request that was submitted to us. In some of the requests for forensic -- for a forensic analysis that we received from the CSB, we were only asked to determine based on the traces and fragments of the projectile to find what projectile that belonged to, and that's what we did. We acted upon those requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was my understanding, too, of your report. Now, once you sent your report to the CSB, would you receive any feedback from them as to what happened with your reports from that moment on? For instance, you would submit a report on the type of ammunition, they didn't ask for your determination on the direction of this projectile, but would you receive any feedback on that report later on?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware or do you know whether -- I see based on your answers that this was not within the purview of your work, but are you aware that at the CSB, the direction of the projectile was sometimes determined based on witness statements, eye-witness statements? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's change the topic. Within your job description or the work that you performed at the Sarajevo MUP, you had to check or search the terrain to ensure that it's secure when an important personality or high official was to visit Sarajevo, and I am talking about the wartime period?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, those were the basic tasks of our department, the anti-sabotage department. This was what we did in wartime, but also in peacetime. This is part of our job description. Our job description did not envisage us conducting on-site investigations because nobody really could foresee what the needs would be in the future. So our basic job description was to provide security for high officials, to prevent possible attacks on a very important individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the war there were such important officials who visited the city of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we also provided security for domestic officials who were entitled to special security. The president, various assembly meetings and so on. So whatever there were high officials, we had to provide for their security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of your work, did you have any closer contacts with members of the BH Army especially with respect to providing security on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just going to ask about the relevancy but my friend now seems to be going into a different area with the questioning so I'll wait. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's just exactly right, but the witness mentioned this in his earlier testimony and in that respect I found this interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So let me repeat my question. In the course of your work, did you have occasion to cooperate with members of the BH Army with respect to security -- providing security in various areas of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the lines of separation were during the war between the two sides, the BH Army and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In some areas of the city, I knew exactly where the separation lines were, and I also had a general idea around town where the lines of separation were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In effect, are you claiming that Sarajevo was surrounded on the perimeter, on the outer borders that it was surrounded by units of the VRS, whereas the inner portions of the town were under the control of the BH Army? Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes. However, some parts of the town were under the control of the VRS throughout the war. For instance, the Grbavica neighbourhood. That was a part of the town abutting on the river, and the river, the Miljacka river was actually the line of separation in the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We understand that, but based on your opinion, when speaking of the expertise, the expert reports, does it mean when you say -- when you indicate that the direction was Trebevic, does this mean that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this witness an expert, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I treat this witness as a fact witness. However, he did provide his expert opinion. When I say expert opinion, perhaps it's better to say his professional opinion that they submitted to the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm only asking because there was mention of expert reports. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, well, let me call it a professional report. That is the term used in the files as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, in your official note when mention is made that, for instance, from the positions of the aggressor on Trebevic, do you agree with me that from that direction there were always also units of the BH Army but they were at a different distance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was always -- there were always lines of separation from the point of impact of the shell and the direction of where the shell had been fired from, or rather, between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see the same map that we've seen earlier, that's P415. Exhibit P415, page 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already explained what these lines mean and what this direction is. This is the incident of the 22nd of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just zoom in on this map a bit. And could we scroll it down, please. No, now we've gone too far. Just a bit higher. Thank you, this is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see on this map a location called Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, would you please assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please put a 1 to indicate this location?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's already a 1 being used on this map. I wonder if we could maybe use an A or something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Could we just put a CK there for Colina Kapa. Could you put a CK, Witness.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this is -- that this territory was at that time under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the lines were in this area approximately. I never went there myself, to be honest, but I believe that the lines were in that general area because Colina Kapa was frequently mentioned in some reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please -- I move to enter this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D73, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, is that D72?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D73, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the immediate vicinity right next to the flea market, there was the factory which produced uniforms for the army and the military?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: For the military and the police, interpreter correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let's discuss the incident itself that you testified to, the incident on the 22nd of December, 1994. You personally attended the on-site investigation following which you analysed the fragments, whereas on the site itself you analysed the crater together with the other members of the team who conducted the on-site investigations; right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And your conclusion was in terms of the type of projectile and its kind, that it was what was stated in the report, that this was an artillery shell, a 76-millimetre artillery shell; correct? Let's discuss this first.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But just to make a distinction so this is not confusing, let's not use artillery. This was actually a projectile, a cannon projectile or a gun projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a specific type of projectile. You did not attend many on-site investigations where you could determine that such a projectile was used or such a projectile produced a crater?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not many. But perhaps I could add that the 76-millimetre gun - I know this although I did not attend the on-site investigation - that the medical centre was shelled with this and these were anti-armour projectiles. A number of those actually impacted on the centre while I was there in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. But do you know, first of all, that this round, the 76-millimetre round, is fired from a cannon or anti-aircraft gun, do you know what type of gun this is? Maybe there's some mention of it made in the report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a military or ballistics expert, but based on the type of projectile, we can determine what weapons they are fired from. As far as I can recall this was a mountain cannon or a mountain gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the maximum angle of the barrel of that gun can be during firing such a round?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I could not tell you without the tables, the firing tables, but as a matter of course, there is a range of the angles from which a projectile can be fired from such a cannon. There could be a lower and -- a minimum and a maximum angle. This would depend on the ground and the terrain, so there would be a minimum and maximum angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you agree with me that this is a rather important parameter to determine the angle of impact and once that angle is determined and if you can determine the angle of firing, then it is also possible to determine the distance from which it was fired?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you know exactly the angle of impact without any additional information it is not possible to determine exactly where the round was fired from because we never had that information from which position a certain projectile was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted to know. So the charge of the projectile is an important parameter in order to determine the distance?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Without that parameter, it is impossible to determine the distance from which a shell was fired. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that you can determine based on the fragments on the type of projectile, but in addition to that, as a person who needs to determine all the other parameters to determine the distance, you need to know whether the charge is a fuller or a heavier or a lighter charge?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. To determine precisely the position from which a round was fired, you have to have information on the type of charge that was used when it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Could we now take a look at your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is now Exhibit 52217. P52217.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this document to be shown on the screen -- P2217. If a fragment that you were analysing was specific in some way that would -- something important that would determine its description, you would need to put that in your report. For instance, the fragments that you found, the stabilisers, so on, you would describe that in the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Not always. Not necessarily. Not necessarily because for a while I prepared these reports myself, I worked on them, completed them, and there was such an abundance of information that it was physically impossible to produce a detailed account so at first we did not provide detailed descriptions of all these factors, later on we did. You could even find some reports from the earlier period that did not even bear the initials of the person who prepared them. But as time went on they became more detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please scroll up the first page of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will also move on to the next page but let's just agree on this, there is no detailed description of the trace evidence that you were to analyse; correct? There are no materiel traces; correct.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now read the second paragraph word for word, and this has to do with the question that was put by Ms. Bolton: "Based on the shell fragments that were gathered at the scene, it was concluded that they belonged to two contact fuse high explosive shells, 76-millimetre calibre, M-70 type shells with UTI M68 fuses." That's what it says there; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It cannot be determined based on this sentence because you did not mention that, that parts of the fuses were found and that they were examined or that whether you found it and examined it. You only state here that this is the type of shell that is used -- the type of fuse that is used with this type of shell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. When we did not -- if we did not have portions of the fuse, it would not be entered in the report. I don't know what photographs show, the photographs from the scene, and I'm sure that in those photographs you could see recognisable portions of the fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I wanted to check here with you. There are two photographs that show fragments found on the spot. We'll take a look at both of them and see what we can deduce from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 33 in B/C/S of this document. I apologise, this is P415, page 33. The photograph on that page. That's the B/C/S version. The B/C/S page. Page 33. This is it. Could we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise on this photograph anything that would indicate that this is a 76-millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: It is very difficult. I don't think anyone would be able to do that from the photograph alone. But when we analyse these, we would have the traces, the trace evidence. We had parts of -- fragments of the fuses and we would look for characteristic elements or fragments that could indicate what shell was in question. In other words, there would be the guidance rings, those portions of the guidance rings, or the tail-fin. The tread on the guidance rings would be different depending on the size of the projectile because each projectile has a characteristic tread. Based on this photograph, however, especially as it's in black and white, you cannot really determine anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, these photographs are colour photographs but obviously during scanning the colour was lost. So in any case, on the basis of this photograph alone, you could not point to a fragment that would indicate that this is this type of shell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Based on this photograph, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let's just take a look at the second photograph. That's page 44, and I will be wrapping up. The same question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't feel under pressure, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understand the Plenary Session is important and I have to finish on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, witness, can you see anything on this photograph that would indicate -- that would be any indication?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can see a damaged part of a fuse, and I can also see something that looks like it's in blue, it is possible that these blue fragments, that they might be the fragments of the guidance rings because they are usually copper made on these types of projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please just indicate the portion of the fuse that you recognise in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, Mr. Usher, you could assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please be patient, the usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just zoom in a bit and then Mr. Usher, could you please assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please put a circle around the fuse?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in this photograph you can recognise that this is the fuse that is used exclusively for 76-millimetre shells?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that I recognise it based on this photograph. Based on it this photograph, you can see that this is the body of the fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't know what type of fuse it is?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, without the markings on it, no. Each fuse would have the marking on it and you not see that in this photograph. Maybe it's on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the marking -- and there was nothing except the description of the fuse itself, there was nothing else in the report that you put -- that you submitted; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We just said that it is a fuse and that's uncontested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But what I showed you earlier and something that was stated in your opinion was that this type of fuse was part of the 76-millimetre shell, but not that this was find on the scene itself; correct? That's what it said in the report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, what it said in the report is that this was -- that the fragments were fragments of this projectile, I don't know exactly how it's worded in the report, but that was the sense, the meaning of it, that all the fragments are consistent with that projectile and this fuse was a fuse that was found on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, could we just enter this into evidence. I was just reminded by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is page 44. This photograph is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D74, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Sir, we are not done with your testimony just yet, unfortunately. And unfortunately we are not going to be able to sit for the third session this afternoon. So the matter is going to stand adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in courtroom II. If you could be in courtroom II tomorrow morning at 9.00, please. May I just warn you that while you are still testifying and you are going for a break, you may not discuss this case with anybody. Not even with your counsel. Okay. Until you finish testifying. Thank you very much. Then the matter stands adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00, courtroom II. Court adjourned.
